title: Why Liquid Grease Solidifies Inside Kitchen Drain Pipes
description: An educational breakdown showing how warm liquid fats and oils cool down and accumulate inside kitchen drain pipes and P-traps.
image_prompt: A detailed 3D technical cutaway illustration of a kitchen sink drainage assembly in a vertical 9:16 composition. A clean stainless steel sink strainer sits at the top, connecting to a standard white plastic P-trap beneath the counter. A clean longitudinal cross-section cutaway reveals the interior of the horizontal and curved pipe section. Inside the pipe, a visible layer of off-white, solidified grease and fat buildup coats the inner pipe walls, significantly narrowing the internal diameter where wastewater flows. studio lighting, realistic pipe wall thickness, physically accurate plumbing geometry, photorealistic textures. The main plumbing visual is centrally located with generous clean background space at the top and bottom. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no arrows, no labels.
visual_story: The visual focuses on the interior of a kitchen P-trap cutaway section. The viewer can see how liquid grease, which appears fluid at the sink level, cools down as it travels through the pipework. The cutaway highlights the layer of solidified fat clinging to the pipe walls, clearly demonstrating how the inner diameter of the drain pipe is reduced over time even before a total blockage occurs.

on_image_text.hook: Why Pouring Liquid Fat Clogs Kitchen Pipes
on_image_text.explanation: Hot grease washes down easily as a liquid, but cools rapidly inside cold drain pipes, sticking to the pipe walls.
on_image_text.takeaway: Wipe greasy pans with paper towels or collect oil in a container before washing.
